Content:
One way of solving polynomial inequalities is to use a graphical method.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to solve the inequality [MATH: p(x) \geq 0] where [MATH: y = p(x)] is a polynomial whose graph is sketched below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c99f4944da2da9b93963e3a05e668f49]

Content:
Solving the inequality [MATH: p(x) \geq 0] means finding the intervals where the graph of [MATH: p(x)] is above the [MATH: x]-axis or touching the [MATH: x]-axis. These parts of the graph of [MATH: p(x)] are shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/59dd9fc2fce4a6b1f850ae89bbba2a96]

Content:
We see that the function lies on or above the [MATH: x]-axis on the intervals

Content:
[MATH: (-\infty, -3] \quad \textrm{and}\quad [-1,2].]

Content:
Therefore, the solution to the inequality [MATH: p(x) \geq 0] is

Content:
[MATH: x \in (-\infty, -3] \cup [-1,2].]

sections.normalized_html:
To solve the inequality [MATH: P(x) \geq 0,] we need to find the values of [MATH: x] for which the curve [MATH: y=P(x)] lies above the [MATH: x]-axis or touches this axis.

The roots of the polynomial [MATH: P(x) = x^3(x+2)^2(x-2)] are [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x= \pm{2},] where

  • [MATH: x=-2] has multiplicity [MATH: 2,]

  • [MATH: x=0] has multiplicity [MATH: 3,] and

  • [MATH: x=2] is a simple root.

Also, [MATH: P(x)] is a polynomial of degree [MATH: 6] with a positive leading coefficient. So, we can graph the curve as follows:

Since we are interested in solving [MATH: P(x) \geq 0,] we look for the parts of the curve that are above the [MATH: x]-axis or touching the [MATH: x]-axis.

Based on the graph, the solution is [MATH: x \in (-\infty,0] \cup [2, \infty).]
